agent-a0e36f2676477e098.jsonl.narrative:
PROVENANCE. All three files hash-match data_manifest.json exactly. The TSV and xlsx Sheet_001 are row-for-row identical: 543/543 exact matches on each of the 7 shared columns (parent SMILES, both fragments, observed value, and all three estimates) with maximum absolute numeric difference 0.0 and identical row order. observation_id exists only in the TSV (a derived read-order label), and the single extra workbook column in_reference_training_set is bit-exactly the predicate "this observation has an exact database row": 331 both-true, 212 both-false, 0 contradictions. It is not a model train/test split.

The database join is a well-defined function, which had to be established before any comparison. (molecule, fragment1, fragment2) yields 290,664 unique keys over 484,907 rows; 131,063 keys carry 2-20 duplicate rows, but all of those share one bde, one bond_type and one delta_stereo and differ only in bond_index. Zero multi-row keys contain more than one distinct bde (max within-key spread exactly 0.0). No min/max/mean dedup choice can change any number reported here - that multiplicity is symmetric-bond bookkeeping.

QUANTUM CHANNEL. On the 331 observations with an exact database row, the quantum estimate IS the database's own value re-serialised at lower precision, not an independent prediction: median |db - quantum| = 0.0195 kcal/mol, 30.2% within 0.01, 81.0% within 0.1, 92.4% within 0.5 and 100.0% within 1.0 (max 6.999). Seven rows agree to 0.001 kcal/mol, which pins the database row as the shared source. The learned channel disagrees: median 0.1291 (6.6x worse), only 42.3% within 0.1, and 8 rows beyond 1.0 (max 4.768). A paired test confirms it - quantum is closer to the database row on 243 of 331 rows versus 76 for learned (Wilcoxon p=5.8e-17). The 25-row residual tail is concentrated on hydrogen-transfer observations where the database stores one value per symmetry-equivalent key while the quantum channel stores an explicitly evaluated geometry; the residual is mean-zero (+0.019, sd 0.582), so it is sampling inside one source value rather than a systematic offset.

REFERENCE CHANNEL. Confirmed a pure per-(fragment_a,fragment_b) lookup: 539 fragment pairs, 290 distinct values, and 0 pairs carrying more than one distinct value (identical result under ordered, sorted, or RDKit-canonicalised keys). The key is the fragment pair, not the molecule - 86 of 419 molecules carry multiple distinct reference values. Critically, the reference channel shares no value with the database at all (0/543, against 144,147 distinct database values), but 313/543 of its values coincide exactly with an experimental value somewhere in the same file (z=+22.8 against a grid null of 105.9 +- 9.1) while only 1/543 equals its own row's value and 0/543 equals the same pair's value in another molecule. It is an independent draw from the same literature value pool - which is what makes it a usable heterogeneity probe. Its error is larger on the 212 database-unmatched rows (MAE 6.207) than on the 331 matched rows (5.024; Welch p=0.0014), so it is not simply a database proxy.

HETEROGENEITY BOUND. This is the core result. Grouping by parent molecule, the 86 molecules with more than one bond observation show a mean within-molecule experimental spread of 13.42 kcal/mol (median 11.90, max 47.90). That is dominated by genuine chemical differences between different bonds, so it is not directly the reference noise. Applying a permutation null (shuffling experimental values within molecule) gives 16.18, i.e. the observed spread is slightly LOWER than random - molecule identity explains little. Grouping by fragment pair, where chemistry is held much more nearly constant, the 4 repeated pairs show a mean spread of just 1.80 kcal/mol (max 3.90). That is the tightest direct evidence, but n=4.

Three independent estimators that make no assumption about which bond is which converge on 1-sigma reference scatter of about 1.6-2.1 kcal/mol: (i) within-bin scatter using tight windows on the quantum estimate gives 2.75 (the quantum channel's own within-bin SD is only 0.14-0.27, so the window really is tight); (ii) a matched-pair estimator over 1002 pairs with |delta quantum| <= 0.1 gives 2.851 with CI [2.658, 3.050]; (iii) a variance decomposition gives sigma_ref = 2.833 with CI [2.455, 3.202] and is exactly self-consistent (predicted sd(quantum-learned) = 2.2445 versus observed 2.2445, ratio 1.0000). The variance decomposition says 88.5% of the quantum channel's squared error and 66.8% of the learned channel's is attributable to the experimental reference values, not to the estimators.

THE FLOOR. A perfect estimator scored against these experimental values would still show MAE = sigma_ref * sqrt(2/pi) = 2.26 kcal/mol under a Gaussian assumption, or 1.54-1.91 kcal/mol using the empirical (heavy-tailed, excess kurtosis 3.48) shape of the observed discrepancies. The Gaussian form is self-refuting as a floor: it lies ABOVE the measured quantum MAE of 2.098, and a floor cannot exceed an observed MAE. The honest headline is therefore a floor of roughly 2.0 kcal/mol, with a defensible range of 1.5-2.0. Below that, this benchmark cannot distinguish two channels. The two calibrated channels are in fact indistinguishable there: quantum MAE 2.098 versus learned 2.411, a gap of only 0.313 kcal/mol = 0.16-0.20 x the floor, and this sample's minimum detectable difference at 80% power is 0.215 kcal/mol. The reference channel (MAE 5.486, 3.57 x the floor) is clearly worse and IS distinguishable.

OBSERVATION VERSUS INFERENCE. Directly observed: the hashes, the 543/543 column matches, the 331/212 train-flag correspondence, the count 331 matched rows, the agreement fractions and medians above, the 539-pair / 290-value / 0-multi-value reference structure, the 86-molecule and 4-pair spreads, and the absence of exact replicates. Inferred: that the quantum channel is a re-serialised database value (from 81% agreement within 0.1 and 100% within 1.0 - strong but not a documented statement); that the experimental values carry ~1.6-2.1 kcal/mol of 1-sigma heterogeneity; and hence that the floor is about 2 kcal/mol and the channel ranking is unresolvable. What the data cannot settle: the SOURCE of the heterogeneity (no method, temperature, or solvent fields exist, so measurement error, phase, and genuine chemical difference cannot be separated), and the fact that the quantum MAE falls below the Gaussian floor implies the experimental values are partly correlated with the database values - meaning the true floor is somewhat below 2.26, favouring the empirical 1.5-1.9 estimates, but the degree of that correlation is not quantifiable from these files alone. The floor is stated as a range for exactly this reason.
caveats: The headline floor is stated as a range (1.5-2.0 kcal/mol), not a point, because the Gaussian-form estimate (2.260) exceeds the observed quantum MAE (2.098) and is therefore refuted as a floor. A floor cannot exceed an observed MAE; the empirical shape-preserving estimates (1.54-1.91) are the ones consistent with all three observed channel MAEs.

The fact that the quantum channel's MAE sits BELOW the Gaussian-form floor is arithmetically impossible for an independent scorer and implies the experimental values are partly correlated with the database values (both ultimately trace to related literature). This means the true floor is below 2.26 and the 1.5-1.9 empirical estimates should be preferred, but the degree of correlation cannot be quantified from these files.

The variance decomposition (sigma_ref = 2.833) assumes the quantum and learned errors are mutually uncorrelated and uncorrelated with the reference noise. The quantum channel's error is nearly the reference noise itself (variance share 0.885), so its own residual is small and the assumption is weak but untestable within the workspace. The matched-pair and within-bin estimators make no such assumption and give the same 2.7-2.9 answer, which is the main reason the conclusion is robust to it.

The 543 bond observations are NOT independent: 419 unique parent molecules, only 4 repeated fragment pairs, and 0 exact replicates. Bond-observation statistics (n=543) are the analysis unit used throughout, and the molecule-level resampling robustness check (sigma_ref 2.829 +- 0.098) is the one that respects the real dependence structure.

The within-molecule experimental spread (mean 13.42 kcal/mol) is dominated by genuine chemical differences between DIFFERENT bonds in the same molecule, not by reference noise. It is reported as required by the workstream but must not be read as the reference uncertainty; the ~1.8 kcal/mol fragment-pair spread and the ~2.8 kcal/mol matched-pair estimates are the meaningful signals, with the caveat that only 4 fragment pairs have repeated observations.

The SOURCE of the reference heterogeneity is unresolvable in this workspace. The files carry no method, temperature, phase, or solvent fields, so measurement error, phase/solvent differences, and genuine chemical difference between nominally identical bonds cannot be separated. The floor is a magnitude, not a mechanism.

Two earlier scripts (ws5_part3.py, and an early ws5_forensic2.py) timed out at 120 s because Python-level set/dict construction and groupby over object-dtype string keys on the 484,907-row database is slow in this environment. They were replaced by vectorised factorize/lexsort/searchsorted equivalents; the final numbers come from those completed runs. No result was estimated or carried over from an incomplete run.

A floor cannot be validated against ground truth here because no true BDE values exist in the workspace. It is established by convergence of four methods plus the self-consistency constraint, not by external reference.

agent-a1e84492c321618f5.jsonl.narrative:
The database is a large but structurally narrow resource: 484,907 raw rows resolve to 42,577 molecules and 290,664 unique (molecule,fragment1,fragment2) fragment pairs, with 144,147 distinct BDE values. The three units are genuinely distinct and must not be conflated. The row/pair redundancy factor is 1.6683, and a single class drives essentially all of it: C-H contributes 171,858 of the 194,243 surplus rows (88.5%) at 2.145 rows per pair, because symmetry-equivalent hydrogens (four H in methane, three in a methyl) generate several rows with identical fragments and identical bde. Every other class sits near 1.0-1.5. I verified that bond_type and bde are constant inside all 290,664 pair units, so the pair unit is well defined, and that no rows are lost by deduplicating. The practical consequence is that any row-weighted average silently over-weights C-H and, within C-H, over-weights symmetric molecules: the C-H class mean moves by 1.70 kcal/mol (96.45 row-weighted vs 98.16 pair-weighted), while other classes move by under 1 kcal/mol.

The structural domain is bounded by two facts: the element set is exactly {C, N, O} with no S, P or halogen anywhere, and the parent heavy-atom count spans only 1 to 10, with 87.5% of molecules at HAC >= 8 and a mean of 8.89. This is a dense, small-molecule database. BDE summaries computed as ordinary unweighted means on unique-pair units give the expected chemistry: O-O weakest at 41.38 kcal/mol, then N-O 58.96 and N-N 62.18, the carbon-heteroatom bonds in the mid 80s-90s, and C-H/H-O strongest near 98-102. O-O has the smallest sample (298 pairs) and the widest relative spread, and its minimum is physically odd at -0.87 kcal/mol.

The coverage boundary is a size boundary, not a chemistry boundary. The HAC cutoff is 10: 150 of 543 benchmark observations (27.6%) have a parent with HAC between 11 and 38, and all of them lie outside the database. By contrast, element coverage explains nothing - 0 of 543 observations involve an element absent from the database, and every benchmark parent is built only from C, N and O, exactly the database element set. Exact fragment-pair coverage is 331/543 (61.0%) and parent-molecule coverage is 369/543 (68.0%). The remaining 174 out-of-database observations split into 150 that are size-incompatible (HAC > 10) and 24 that are size-compatible (HAC <= 10) yet simply absent.

The most consequential finding is that the database is not exhaustive even inside its own domain. Conditioning on the 369 observations whose parent molecule does exist in the database, only 331 (89.7%) have the exact fragment pair; 38 (10.3%) do not. I checked these are real gaps and not SMILES-writing mismatches: for C#CC#C the database stores only the C-C bond while the benchmark asks for the C-H bond, and for C=CC=C the database has only the C-C bond while the benchmark asks for C-H. Scaling this up, I compared each molecule's stored pair count against its symmetry-unique bond count (H-added, canonical bond orbits): pooled completeness is 52.0% over a random 2,000-molecule sample and 65.0% over the 259 benchmark parents present in the database, with only 1.65% of sampled molecules fully enumerated. So the database is a partial bond selection - roughly half to two-thirds of the available bonds per molecule - rather than a complete bond inventory. Any residual analysis that treats a non-matching benchmark row as evidence about quantum or learned model error will conflate genuine model error with a missing reference entry, which is why the distinction between the 331 exact matches and the 38 parent-present-but-pair-absent rows matters downstream.

Methodological caveat worth carrying forward: an intermediate version of this analysis built the molecule-to-HAC map from database molecules only, so the 174 benchmark parents absent from the database received NaN HAC and the "observations beyond the HAC cutoff" count came out as a spurious 0. The delivered artifact recomputes HAC and element sets for all 419 benchmark parents directly with RDKit, giving 150.
caveats: The bond-class census uses the database's own bond_type column, not a re-derived label. Exhaustively relabeling all 206,797 distinct fragment strings with RDKit would take ~32 min (measured 9.3 ms per parse), so the labeler was validated instead on 4,000 random unique pairs, agreeing 100.0% with bond_type. The census counts therefore inherit any error present in the source bond_type column.

The exhaustiveness test compares stored pair counts against symmetry-unique bond orbits on the H-added graph. A modest fraction of sampled molecules yield more stored pairs than orbits (ratio slightly above 1.0), which would happen if some stored fragments are not atom-permutation-symmetric, so completeness is capped at 1.0 and the reported figures are conservative lower bounds on the true shortfall.

HAC is computed from the parent SMILES string with RDKit GetNumHeavyAtoms; a different SMILES protonation or tautomer choice for the same compound would shift its HAC, and 23 molecule-agnostic fragment pairs are shared across two different molecule strings.

The 543 experimental reference values come from heterogeneous literature and are not independent repeats from one laboratory. All benchmark-unit statistics here are counts over observations, not over independent physical measurements; unique-molecule counts are reported separately (419 unique parents).

The exhaustiveness completeness measure treats every symmetry-unique bond as an equally expected entry, which is an assumption about what an exhaustive database should contain; the real upstream database may deliberately exclude certain bond types or unstable fragments, so the 52-65% figures measure departure from full bond enumeration rather than a documented curation rule.

The 543-row benchmark and the 484,907-row database overlap only partially by construction: 174 benchmark observations have no database parent at all, so any downstream error analysis must be conditioned on the 369/331 inside-domain subsets and cannot treat the 174 as model failures.

An intermediate run had a real bug: HAC for benchmark parents absent from the database mapped to NaN, silently zeroing the HAC-boundary count. Fixed before writing the deliverable; all reported coverage numbers come from the corrected run and were re-verified with an independent raw-CSV/raw-TSV code path.

WS6 tried to break the other workstreams' claims and largely failed to break the important ones - but it did break the single most quotable one. Eight checks plus two extra adversarial probes were executed; five passed, three failed.

The reference channel is genuinely, robustly the worst estimator. Its MAE of 5.49 kcal/mol is more than double the other two, it ranks last in all 419 leave-one-molecule-out fits, in every outlier trim, in every leave-one-bond-class-out fit, on all six error definitions, and on both the unique-fragment-pair subset and the 331 database-matched rows. Nothing in this suite moves it.

The coverage-boundary claim also survives intact, and for a structural reason worth stating plainly: the database heavy-atom maximum is exactly 10 with zero molecules above it, so the boundary is a hard domain edge, not a soft cut-off whose value someone chose. The competing thresholds only change how LARGE the uncovered benchmark region is (150 observations above HAC 10, 136 above 11, 111 above 12), never whether it exists. Redefining size by RDKit molecular weight reproduces the same conclusion (DB max 152.1 Da, 138 observations / 25.4% above), and benchmark HAC and MolWt correlate at Spearman 0.996, so the two definitions are effectively the same variable here.

The headline "quantum beats learned" claim is where the suite bites. It is fragile in three independent ways. First, it is test-dependent: the mean absolute-error difference is solidly nonzero (paired t p = 5.4e-5, both row and molecule-cluster bootstrap CIs exclude zero), but the Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p = 0.553, the within-2-kcal McNemar test p = 0.078, and - the sharpest finding - learned wins on 284 of 543 observations versus quantum's 246. Quantum wins on the mean while learned wins on the majority of individual bonds; the mean advantage is a thinner-extreme-tail effect (quantum's worst error 15.7 vs learned's 25.2 kcal/mol), not a typical-bond effect. Second, and decisively, the effect is not distributed across the benchmark at all: it is carried entirely by the 158 observations that are simultaneously HAC >= 10 and have no exact database row (diff -1.131 kcal/mol, CI [-1.603, -0.695]). In the other three cells of that 2x2 the difference is indistinguishable from zero, and on the 331 in-database rows it changes sign (+0.064 kcal/mol, learned if anything better). Dropping the HAC 10+ bin outright flips the ranking to learned (1.811) < quantum (1.829). Third, the test-choice sensitivity means any summary phrased as "quantum is the better estimator" must state whether it means the mean or the typical bond, because the two disagree.

One methodological check came out the opposite of what I expected, and it is a genuine pass for the other workstreams. Resampling whole molecules (419 units) instead of rows (543 units) leaves every confidence interval essentially unchanged - the q-vs-l cluster CI [-0.473, -0.168] versus the row CI [-0.471, -0.168]. The 86 multi-row molecules share fragments but evidently not correlated errors, so the row-level paired analysis was not overstating precision. Likewise, no single molecule moved any channel's MAE by more than 0.052 kcal/mol, so the ranking is not an artefact of one clustered molecule.

The largest cluster-free subset (one row per molecule, 419 independent-ish units) actually strengthens the mean result: MAE rises to 2.28 / 2.72 / 5.75, and the q-vs-l gap widens from -0.313 to -0.437 kcal/mol. So the fragility of the quantum-vs-learned claim is not an artefact of pseudo-replication - it is genuine heterogeneity between the in-database and out-of-database regions of the benchmark, which is the more interesting scientific statement.

Explicit per-check status: 1 leave-one-molecule-out PASS; 2 alternative error definitions PASS; 3 outlier treatment PASS; 4 batch/class leave-out FAIL (no class effect, but a decisive size/database-batch effect); 5 threshold sensitivity PASS; 6 paired-unit sensitivity PASS; 2b test-choice sensitivity FAIL; 4b HAC x database-membership split FAIL.

Verdict list: reference worse than both ROBUST; quantum beats learned on MAE FRAGILE; quantum and learned not distinguishable FRAGILE (false on the mean, true per typical bond); database covers only HAC<=10 ROBUST; 331/543 exact-row split ROBUST; quantum reproduces the database BDE ROBUST; 9-class bond-class error structure NOT TESTABLE; database exhaustive within its own domain ROBUST; held-out degradation measurable FRAGILE (real for all channels, but the q-vs-l ordering inverts out of database).

For the downstream workstreams: WS1's coverage boundary and WS5's provenance claims are safe as stated. WS2's headline should be re-phrased to name its summary statistic and to report the mean-vs-majority reversal, and its item-5 training/held-out split should carry the warning that the q-vs-l ordering inverts there. WS3's class-comparison claim is untestable on this benchmark, not merely under-powered: only two bond classes have usable n (C-H 302, C-C 240) and the H-O cell has n = 1.

TAIL CENSUS (unit = bond observation, n=543). The three channels have very different hard boundaries. Quantum's worst cases (obs 0403, 0491, 0487) share a readable motif: carboxylic-acid C-C cleavage whose surviving radical is [O=C]O; 5 of its 8 rows beyond 10 kcal/mol are this motif, all overshoots of +10.8 to +15.7. Reference's hard boundary is therefore two opposite-signed cliffs, not one tail.

Learned is strong: ring count 2.08 vs 0.93 (p=1.4e-10, BH q=1.2e-9, Cliff's delta 0.444), fused rings 2.01 vs 0.90 (q=1.9e-9), HAC 13.0 vs 8.7 (q=1.5e-8), aromatic rings 1.30 vs 0.63 (q=7.4e-6), heteroatoms 0.85 vs 0.37 (q=1.4e-4), fsp3 lower in failures (0.41 vs 0.55). The headline structural fact is coverage, not error. The 543-observation benchmark contains only three of the nine bond classes present in the 484907-row database: C-H (n=302), C-C (n=240) and H-O (n=1). C-N, C-O, H-N, N-N, N-O and O-O are entirely absent even though together they are 16.5% of database rows. The WS3 mandate to characterise error by chemical bond class therefore collapses to a single two-way comparison, C-H versus C-C. The labeler is trustworthy where testable: it reproduces the database bond_type on all 331 matched rows, and an independent raw-SMILES element scan agrees (only one row has an O radical centre).

On the two populated classes the three channels rank consistently - quantum best (MAE 2.098, bias +0.554), learned next (2.411, +1.079), reference much worse (5.486, +1.378). The reference channel's deficit is almost entirely a bias problem: its RMSE (6.760) is only 1.15x the learned channel's but its MAE is 2.28x, because its errors are systematically signed rather than scattered. That is the signature of an offset, not noise.

Bond class is NOT the dominant determinant of error - molecule size is, for all three channels. R2 on |error| is 0.0030-0.0035 for class alone versus 0.0456-0.1818 for parent heavy-atom count; adding class on top of size buys at most 0.0146 (quantum), 0.0046 (learned, permutation p=0.098) and 0.0001 (reference, p=0.822). The size trend survives within a fixed class (quantum MAE rises 1.76 -> 1.81 -> 2.20 for C-H and 1.61 -> 1.97 -> 3.82 for C-C across HAC <=5 / 6-9 / >=10), so it is not an artifact of pooling. The C-H/C-C contrast is further undermined by a direction flip: at HAC<=5 C-C is better, at HAC>=10 C-H is better (quantum 2.20 vs 3.82, p=0.005). Class and size are confounded in the sample anyway - C-H bonds live in larger parents (median HAC 9 vs 7, p<1e-8), and the HAC>=10 bin is 75.7% C-H but only 23.8% C-C. The honest statement is that no robust class main effect exists here apart from one exception below.

That exception is real: the reference channel's bias flips sign between classes, +5.103 kcal/mol on C-H versus -3.303 on C-C (difference 8.406, Welch t=18.2). It over-estimates C-H bonds and under-estimates C-C bonds, and this single fact explains why its pooled MAE is 2.6x the quantum channel's. Only the arithmetic matters here; the data contain no metadata on how the reference channel was built, so no mechanism is asserted.

The strongest failure axis measurable from this data alone is bond strength. Error is markedly heteroscedastic (Levene p=0.0 for quantum and learned, 5.7e-5 for reference) and every channel degrades toward the weak-bond end: below 70 kcal/mol MAE is 5.997 / 7.527 / 7.939 with large positive bias (+4.57 / +6.87), versus 1.670 / 1.638 / 4.938 in the 85-100 window where quantum and learned are nearly unbiased (+0.10 / +0.19). A limitation I flag rather than hide: the <70 bin contains zero HAC<=5 observations and is shifted to larger parents (median HAC 12.5 vs 8.0), so weak-bond and large-molecule failure are globally confounded. The one cell that holds both class and size fixed and still has enough weak rows - C-C / HAC>=10, 12 weak vs 34 other - does show the effect surviving (quantum 7.663 vs 2.468, learned 9.268 vs 2.513), but that is a single cell and should be treated as suggestive rather than established.

Environment effects measurable without external data are mostly a learned-channel story. Nitrogen-containing parents raise its error to 4.902 (n=37) vs 2.229, with a bootstrap CI excluding zero and the effect persisting inside C-H alone (4.551 vs 2.312) - so it is a genuine composition effect, not a class artifact. Benzene rings and ring-member radical centres push the learned channel up in the same direction (3.195 vs 1.876; 3.096 vs 2.063), with the quantum channel following weakly and the reference channel largely flat to aromaticity. The reference channel is the only one that improves anywhere: on oxygen-containing parents its MAE falls to 4.538 from 5.791. Sulfur (n=0) and aromatic radical centres (n=10, of which only 3 C-C) are too thin to say anything about, and I record them in the thin-sample ledger rather than asserting an effect.

Concrete applicability boundary. Within the measured domain (C-H and C-C bonds only, 419 parent molecules), the best region for all three channels is small-parent C-C bonds, C-C / HAC<=5 (n=61): quantum MAE 1.607, learned 1.448, reference 4.389. The worst is large-parent C-C, C-C / HAC>=10 (n=46): quantum 3.824, learned 4.275, reference 7.763. Adding the magnitude axis, the worst 3-way cell is C-C / HAC>=10 / <70 kcal/mol (n=12): quantum 7.663, learned 9.268; the best powered cell is C-C / HAC<=5 / 85-100 kcal/mol (n=29): quantum 1.321, learned 1.201. Practically: these channels are usable (MAE ~1.3-1.7 kcal/mol) on small-to-medium C-H and C-C bonds of normal strength, and should not be trusted below ~70 kcal/mol or on parents above ~10 heavy atoms, where MAE approaches 8-9 kcal/mol - roughly a factor of 5 degradation. Nothing in this workstream supports extrapolating any of it to the six unrepresented bond classes.
caveats: The benchmark's 543 rows are heterogeneous literature bond observations, not independent repeats from one lab; experimental reference uncertainty is not propagated, so all MAEs are lower bounds on true error against a perfect reference.

Bond-class coverage is the binding limitation: only C-H and C-C are populated (plus a single H-O row). Six of nine database bond classes have zero benchmark coverage, so the requested 'error by bond class' table is effectively a two-class comparison. No class-level claim is made for C-N, C-O, H-N, N-N, N-O or O-O.

H-O has n=1 and is reported only for completeness - no inference is drawn. That single row also happens to be the largest parent in the sample (HAC=22), so its numbers are not representative of anything.

Analysis units are distinct: 543 bond observations, 419 unique parent molecules, 543 unique (parent, fragment_a, fragment_b) triples (539 unique unordered fragment pairs). All per-class n values in the JSON count bond observations unless the field name says otherwise. Many observations share a parent, so observations are not mutually independent.
Class and size are confounded (C-H median HAC 9 vs C-C 7, Mann-Whitney p<1e-8), and the HAC>=10 bin is 75.7% C-H. Marginal class comparisons are therefore not clean.

Weak-bond (<70 kcal/mol) and large-molecule failure are also confounded: the weak bin has zero HAC<=5 rows and median HAC 12.5 vs 8.0 overall. Only one cell (C-C / HAC>=10) supports testing the magnitude effect with class and size held fixed, and it is a single cell.
OLS R2 on |error| is descriptive only. Residuals are skewed and heteroscedastic (Levene p<=5.7e-5), so R2 magnitudes are small and must not be read as a predictive model or as effect sizes.

Environment flags (aromaticity, ring membership, N/O content, benzene) are correlated with each other and with parent size; the stratified tables control only one factor at a time, so the reported flag effects are not mutually adjusted.

Aromatic radical centre (n_true=10) and sulfur-containing parents (n_true=0) are too thin to support any claim; they are recorded in the thin-sample ledger with n<10 flagged explicitly rather than interpreted.

The reference-channel bias sign flip between C-H and C-C is a measured property of this benchmark's reference channel. The data contain no metadata on the reference channel's construction, so no mechanism is asserted.

The 70-85 kcal/mol bin is the largest (n=246) and sits around the median (85.3), so the pooled MAE is dominated by that region; this is a sampling property of the benchmark, not a weighting choice of this analysis.

The three channels are not three estimates of equal quality - they are two. Quantum (MAE 2.098, RMSE 3.060) and learned (2.411, 3.628) are near-duplicates: their estimates correlate at r=0.985, their signed errors agree in sign 86.6 percent of the time, and their absolute errors correlate at 0.754. Reference (5.486, 6.760) is a genuinely separate estimator whose absolute errors correlate with the other two at only about 0.21 and 0.20, with partial correlations of 0.05-0.10 once shared difficulty is removed. It is not simply worse at the same hard bonds; it is bad at mostly different bonds. Reference is the best channel on only 28 of 543 observations and the worst on 345.

On the paired question, the reference comparisons are decisive and need no hedging: quantum beats reference by 3.39 kcal/mol of MAE (Cliff's delta -0.631) and learned beats reference by 3.08 (delta -0.573), with every test at p below 1e-49.

Quantum vs learned is the interesting result and the honest answer is NOT DISTINGUISHABLE at this sample size for the typical observation. The mean absolute-error difference is -0.313 kcal/mol (95 percent CI -0.471 to -0.165; paired t p=5.4e-5), but the median difference is +0.020 kcal/mol (Wilcoxon p=0.553, sign test p=0.108, Cliff's delta -0.042) and learned actually has the smaller absolute error on more observations (284 vs 246, 13 ties), with a typical discordant gap of only 0.24 kcal/mol. The mean is being pulled by asymmetric tails, and capping absolute error at 15, 10, 7.5, 5 or 3 kcal/mol barely moves it, so it is not a single-outlier artefact - but a mean that disagrees with the median, Wilcoxon, sign test and headcount is a weak basis for a ranking claim. The split is driven by where you look: quantum wins clearly on held-out molecules (mean difference -0.901) and ties in-sample (+0.064, CI touching zero), and wins clearly in the weak-bond quartiles (-0.856, -0.399) while tying in the strong ones. By bond class the entire quantum advantage is in C-H (-0.551); C-C is a dead heat (-0.002). Bottom line: quantum is the better default because it strictly dominates on the out-of-sample half and is never worse, but the in-sample difference is not established.

Calibration explains the reference channel's failure mode. Quantum (slope 0.932) and learned (0.891) are compressed toward the mean and both significantly so (p below 1e-12 versus slope 1); reference (1.073) is amplified (p=5.8e-4). Compression means the two machine channels overestimate weak bonds (mean signed error +2.90 and +5.11 kcal/mol in the weakest decile) and are nearly unbiased for strong ones, so their error concentrates at the LOW end of the range, not the high end - MAE 3.75 and 5.37 in the weakest decile versus 1.89 and 2.06 in the middle 80 percent. This matches the common practice of fitting these models to a high-BDE-dominated set: they regress toward the training mean. Reference's amplification produces the opposite signature, overestimating strong bonds (+4.17 kcal/mol in the top decile) and producing the single worst error in the whole benchmark (-33.4 kcal/mol).

The training split is the closest available out-of-sample test, and it is more nuanced than a simple degradation ranking. Aggregate MAE rises for all three (quantum 1.87 to 2.45, +31 percent; learned 1.81 to 3.35, +86 percent; reference 5.02 to 6.21, +24 percent), which would suggest learned overfits most. But stratifying by bond class breaks that story: on C-H, quantum and reference show literally zero degradation (p=0.70 and 0.98) while learned still degrades sharply (1.95 to 3.08, p=3.6e-5); on C-C all three roughly double. Since the held-out set is 75 percent C-H while the training set is 56 percent C-C, most of quantum's and reference's aggregate decay is a composition effect rather than overfitting. Separately, 4 held-out rows fall outside the training experimental range (61.4-160.2 kcal/mol) and are catastrophically mispredicted by all three (MAE 11.3-15.1 kcal/mol), but account for only about 29, 15 and 8 percent of quantum's, learned's and reference's aggregate degradation. So learned's out-of-sample decay is the one that survives every control; the others' is largely compositional.

Two caveats constrain all of the above. First, the experimental values are heterogeneous literature values, not independent repeats, so the 543 rows are 543 bond observations and not 543 independent measurements - the effective sample size for any ranking is smaller than the nominal p-values imply, which makes the null quantum-vs-learned result the more conservative reading. Second, the reference channel's errors being nearly uncorrelated with the other two means the three channels are not exchangeable and an ensemble or consensus estimate is a plausible next step rather than a curiosity; 9 observations sit in all three channels' worst decile simultaneously, 33 where quantum and learned both do, but only 14 where quantum and reference both do.
caveats: The 543 experimental values are heterogeneous literature values, NOT independent repeats from one lab. All p-values in this workstream treat rows as independent samples, so nominal significance is overstated. The rank/sign tests (which give the null quantum-vs-learned answer) are less affected than the paired t-test because they do not depend on tail magnitudes.

The quantum-vs-learned comparison gives a genuinely split verdict and I did not force it to a winner. The paired t-test on the mean absolute-error difference is significant (p=5.4e-5) while the Wilcoxon (p=0.553), sign test (p=0.108) and headcount (246 vs 284) are not. Quoting only the t-test overstates the case; quoting only the Wilcoxon understates it.

The in_reference_training_set split is a provenance split (row present in the source DB), not a randomised held-out set. The two subsets differ in bond-class composition (train 56 percent C-C, held-out 75 percent C-H), in experimental mean (89.7 vs 82.6 kcal/mol, Welch p=5.1e-10) and in range (held-out extends to 15.2 kcal/mol, below anything in training). Degradation estimates are therefore confounded with composition; stratified and range-restricted versions of every degradation number are reported in the JSON.

The H-O bond class contains a single observation, so its paired t-test is undefined (paired_t_p is null in the JSON) and its Wilcoxon p=1.0 is uninformative. It is flagged with a _note field and must not be used as evidence. C-H and C-C together are 542 of 543 rows, so the benchmark is effectively a two-class problem.
Bootstrap CIs and tests were seeded (20260919) for reproducibility, but bootstrap resampling of 543 literature-derived rows does not create information that is not there.

Degradation comparisons between the training and held-out subsets use Welch and Mann-Whitney tests on disjoint groups of DIFFERENT observations, not a paired design, because the same bond never appears in both subsets. They are between-group comparisons and carry the composition confounding described above.

The reference channel's slope of 1.073 is significantly above 1 but its 95 percent CI lower bound is 1.032, so the amplification is modest; the compression of quantum (0.932) and learned (0.891) is far more precisely determined.
